title: KPIs, variables, grain, chart and data-story critique

sections.title: How to use this toolkit
sections.html:
Read Sections 1–5 in order. Section 1 turns a managerial question into a decision and a KPI. Section 2 establishes what one data row represents. Section 3 checks simple relationships and reproduces them in Excel 365 and SPSS. Section 4 critiques a proposed chart. Section 5 builds a bounded management story. Each section includes an ungraded Try it with an explained answer.

The core crosswalk is analytics framing and basic data vocabulary (H001–H004), plus audience, context, and intended action (H009–H018). Relationship types, business-intelligence tools, measurement, and narrative structure (H005–H008, H019–H024) are taught only where they strengthen this session; the coverage map marks their priority. The course has no required textbook. The listed textbook headings are scope cues, not claims that you have read those chapters. This original synthesis is grounded in the open and primary sources actually cited below.

This source chapter has no stable PDF pages. Use its stable numbered section headings—not guessed page numbers—for future slide or PNP cross-references after pagination. S01 business-question framing is the prerequisite. Distributions and deeper quality work begin in S03; sampling, tests, and causal or predictive models belong to later sessions.

sections.title: A single fictional case: Mosaic Pantry
sections.html:
Mosaic Pantry is fictional. Its operations manager must decide whether to trial a standard order reminder workflow next week. Staff currently send some reminders, but not by a fixed rule. The manager hopes reminders improve on-time handoff without adding excessive preparation pressure.

The intended population is all Mosaic Pantry orders eligible for pickup or delivery during the next operating month. The unit of analysis here is one completed order. The analyst has only the first 12 completed orders exported from two September days. This is a convenience extract, not a random sample of next month’s orders. An order ID is a key: it identifies an order and should occur once at this grain. Definitions of cases, variables, populations, and samples matter because a statistic from selected cases does not automatically describe a wider population (Penn State Department of Statistics, n.d.-a; OpenStax, 2023).

Order IDModeReminder sentOn timeBasket ($)Prep (min)
101PickupYesYes3218
102PickupYesYes4820
103PickupYesYes4022
104PickupYesYes3624
105DeliveryYesYes6030
106DeliveryYesNo5445
107PickupNoYes2519
108PickupNoYes3023
109DeliveryNoYes4532
110DeliveryNoNo5542
111DeliveryNoNo5048
112DeliveryNoNo6552

Source and limits: Treat these as invented rows from an order-system export. “On time” means customer handoff at or before the recorded promise time; “prep” means minutes from order acceptance to ready-for-handoff status. The table does not contain timestamps with which to audit either derived field. It omits cancellations, eligibility for a reminder, and why staff chose to send one. It can support practice in description, not an estimate of reminder impact.

sections.title: 1. Frame the decision before naming the KPI
sections.html: Why these scores: A precise decision, target, and safety boundary make a reported number usable rather than merely interesting.

sections.title: 1.1 Stakeholder, action, and testable claim
sections.html:
A stakeholder uses the analysis; a decision is a choice that stakeholder can make. Here the stakeholder is the operations manager. The immediate choice is whether to run a limited, monitored reminder trial—not whether to announce that reminders work. Before analysis, ask: Who can act? By when? What would change the choice? What would count as harm? These questions distinguish an actionable request from “show me a dashboard.”

Work from question to claim:

  1. Problem: Some customers receive orders after their promised handoff time.
  2. Possible action: Trial a standard reminder workflow.
  3. Observable descriptive claim: In these 12 rows, orders marked “Reminder sent = Yes” have a higher on-time fraction than rows marked “No.”
  4. Future testable impact claim: Under a suitable future comparison, using the workflow improves on-time handoff without breaching a prep-pressure guardrail.

Step 3 can be checked in this extract. Step 4 cannot: staff chose reminders, and the two groups may differ in other ways. This is an observational comparison, not a controlled assignment. Penn State distinguishes observational designs from experiments and warns that another variable can explain an apparent relationship (Penn State Department of Statistics, n.d.-a).

Failure mode: “The manager wants an 80% KPI” is not a testable claim. It says neither which orders count nor what action follows.

Try it — ungraded. A colleague asks, “Can you show that reminders fix late deliveries?” Rewrite this as one question this table can answer.

Explained answer: “Among the completed orders shown, what fraction was on time in the reminder-Yes group and in the reminder-No group?” The answer will describe these rows. It will not establish that sending a reminder fixed anything.

sections.title: 1.2 KPI contract, target, and guardrail
sections.html:
A KPI is a defined measure used to monitor a decision. Give it a contract: population and exclusions, time window, grain, numerator, denominator, units, owner, refresh date, and treatment of missing values. For this exercise, the on-time handoff rate has numerator “completed orders handed off by the recorded promise time” and denominator “completed orders with a recorded promise time and handoff outcome.” Its unit is a percentage of eligible completed orders. Order ID is counted once. A production definition must also decide how to report excluded or missing orders.

A rate without its denominator, exclusions, and time window is not a complete KPI.

For the 12 displayed rows, count eight “Yes” outcomes and 12 completed orders: 8/12×100=66.7%8/12\times100=66.7\%, rounded to one decimal. Suppose the manager’s provisional target is at least 80%. The displayed rate is 80.0−66.7=13.380.0-66.7=13.3 percentage points below that target after rounding. A guardrail monitors a potential cost of the action. Define the provisional prep-pressure guardrail as “no more than 25% of completed orders take over 40 minutes to reach ready status.” Four orders—106, 110, 111, and 112—exceed 40 minutes; 4/12×100=33.3%4/12\times100=33.3\%. That is 8.3 percentage points above the provisional ceiling after rounding. These thresholds are fictional management choices, not statistical findings.

Business interpretation: The displayed completed orders miss both provisional thresholds. Neither number estimates next month’s performance: the extract is small and selected. Nor does prep time by itself measure staff welfare. A manager would first confirm that this guardrail captures the pressure they intend to limit.

Failure mode: Subtracting percentages and calling the result “13.3% worse” confuses a percentage-point gap with a relative percentage change.

Try it — ungraded. If order 112’s prep time were corrected from 52 to 40 minutes, would it breach the stated guardrail definition?

Explained answer: No. The rule says over 40 minutes, not “40 minutes or more.” The numerator would become three and the displayed rate 3/12=25%3/12=25\%, exactly at the ceiling. A one-word definition changes the decision reading.

sections.title: 2. Choose variables and grain before calculating
sections.html: Why these scores: Many misleading reports start with a duplicated unit, an ambiguous field, or a measurement rule that changed midstream.

sections.title: 2.1 Population, observation, variable, and key
sections.html:
An observation is one recorded case; grain states precisely what one row represents. The displayed grain is one completed order, not one customer or one message. A variable can change across observations. Mode and reminder status are categorical labels; basket dollars and prep minutes are quantitative measurements. Order ID looks numeric but is an identifier, not a meaningful quantity: averaging 101 and 102 would not describe a business outcome. These distinctions guide valid summaries (Penn State Department of Statistics, n.d.-a).

Check a proposed input in steps. Suppose a message-system export has two messages for order 101 and one for each of the other 11 orders. Joining every message row to the order table without first deciding the grain would create 13 joined rows. It would count order 101 twice. If both joined copies retain its “On time = Yes” value, the apparent rate becomes 9/13=69.2%9/13=69.2\%, instead of the correct 8/12=66.7%8/12=66.7\%. To protect the order-level KPI, reduce messages to one order-level field—such as whether any qualifying reminder was sent—then check that there is one record per order ID before calculating. This join is an illustrative possible source error; the supplied 12-row table itself has no duplicate ID.

Declare the unit counted in the denominator before combining sources or averaging rows.

Failure mode: Calling 13 joined message rows “13 orders” silently changes the unit and inflates the rate.

Try it — ungraded. If one customer places orders 101 and 102, may both remain in an order-level rate?

Explained answer: Yes. They are distinct orders, so each contributes once to an order-level denominator. A customer-level question would require a new grain and a new rule for summarizing that customer’s orders.

sections.title: 2.2 Operational definitions and provenance
sections.html:
An operational definition tells another analyst exactly how a concept becomes a recorded value. “On time” sounds simple, but pickup ready time is not the same as customer handoff time. For order 106, “Prep = 45” means 45 minutes from acceptance to ready status; “On time = No” means handoff missed the recorded promise. One value does not mechanically determine the other. Provenance records where fields came from and how they were transformed. A credible audit would retain source-system names, extraction period, time zone, timestamp rules, field definitions, transformation steps, and a de-identified order key.

Before trusting the 12 rows, check: Are there 12 unique IDs? Are all outcomes Yes or No? Is prep nonnegative and measured in minutes? Is each promise timestamp present? Were reminder events sent before the relevant handoff? Are cancellations excluded consistently? The displayed table lets us check IDs, visible categories, and prep ranges; it cannot verify source timestamps or omitted orders. Treat the last questions as unresolved, not as passed checks. Measurement errors and selection problems can undermine conclusions even when arithmetic is correct (OpenStax, 2023).

Failure mode: Replacing a missing “On time” outcome with “No” without documenting the rule turns unknown outcomes into apparent failures.

Try it — ungraded. An exported order has a promise time but no handoff timestamp. Should it silently enter the on-time numerator or denominator defined in Section 1.2?

Explained answer: Neither. Its outcome is unknown under that definition. Flag and count the exclusion separately, investigate the source, and show how an alternative missing-data treatment would affect the KPI before using it for a decision.

sections.title: 3. Compare relationships and reproduce the arithmetic
sections.html: Why these scores: A manager needs comparisons with the correct denominators, and another analyst must be able to inspect and repeat them.

sections.title: 3.1 Three relationship shapes; one careful comparison
sections.html:
Choose a summary that fits the variables. Two categorical variables, such as reminder status and on-time outcome, support a two-way count table. A categorical and a numeric variable, such as reminder status and prep minutes, support a group summary. Two numeric variables, such as basket dollars and prep minutes, might support a scatterplot, but a visible pattern would still not establish a cause. These are descriptive relationship shapes, not tests of impact. Penn State’s descriptions of categorical displays and two-way tables provide starting points for the first shape (Penn State Department of Statistics, n.d.-b).

Count the displayed orders by reminder status:

Reminder statusOn timeLateGroup totalOn-time fraction
Yes5165/6=83.3%5/6=83.3\%
No3363/6=50.0%3/6=50.0\%

The descriptive gap is 83.3−50.0=33.383.3-50.0=33.3 percentage points after rounding. Now check a competing explanation: four of six reminder-Yes orders are pickup, but only two of six reminder-No orders are pickup. All six pickup orders are on time; only two of six delivery orders are on time. Mode and reminder status are mixed together in this extract. The table cannot isolate a reminder effect.

For a categorical–numeric summary, add prep minutes for reminder-Yes orders: 18+20+22+24+30+45=15918+20+22+24+30+45=159; divide by six to get 26.5 minutes. For reminder-No orders: 19+23+32+42+48+52=21619+23+32+42+48+52=216; divide by six to get 36 minutes. This is another observation about selected orders, not evidence that reminders shorten prep. Reporting the group counts alongside both means prevents a bare mean from hiding how little data support it. Formal association, uncertainty, and confounding analysis come later in the course.

Failure mode: “83.3% versus 50.0% proves a 33.3% lift caused by reminders.” It confuses percentage points with relative change and an observed difference with causal impact.

Try it — ungraded. What is the delivery-only on-time fraction, regardless of reminder status?

Explained answer: Delivery orders are 105, 106, and 109–112: six orders. Only 105 and 109 are on time, so 2/6=33.3%2/6=33.3\%. The denominator is delivery orders, not all 12 orders.

sections.title: 3.2 Excel 365 and SPSS: same question, independent checks
sections.html:
First specify the calculation. Inputs are 12 order-level records; the output is a count, a percentage, and a mean in minutes. Count each order once. Divide an on-time count by the count of orders in the same reminder group. Divide a group’s prep-minute sum by its order count. Confirm the group counts total 12 and the on-time counts total eight before interpreting either tool’s result.

Excel 365 route. Enter the displayed columns, including headers, in A1:F13 in this order: ID, Mode, Reminder, OnTime, Basket, Prep. Place the following formulas in separate empty cells:

=COUNTIFS(C2:C13,"Yes",D2:D13,"Yes")   // 5 on-time, reminder-Yes orders
=COUNTIF(C2:C13,"Yes")                 // 6 reminder-Yes orders
=COUNTIFS(C2:C13,"Yes",D2:D13,"Yes")/COUNTIF(C2:C13,"Yes")
                                         // 0.833333...; format as 83.3%
=SUMIFS(F2:F13,C2:C13,"Yes")           // 159 prep minutes
=SUMIFS(F2:F13,C2:C13,"Yes")/COUNTIF(C2:C13,"Yes")
                                         // 26.5 minutes per order

The comments after // explain expected results; omit them when entering formulas. Repeat with "No" to obtain 3, 6, 50.0%, 216, and 36 minutes. COUNTIFS counts rows meeting both criteria; SUMIFS adds values meeting a criterion. Microsoft documents these functions and their argument order (Microsoft, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

SPSS route. Enter one case per order, retaining the order ID. Set Reminder and OnTime as categorical fields and Prep as numeric minutes. A transparent syntax version uses exact text values as entered above:

CROSSTABS
  /TABLES=Reminder BY OnTime
  /CELLS=COUNT ROW.
MEANS TABLES=Prep BY Reminder
  /CELLS=COUNT MEAN SUM.

Read the Reminder-Yes row: five Yes outcomes out of six, or 83.3%. The means output should give six cases, 159 minutes in total, and a 26.5-minute mean for that group. IBM documents row percentages for CROSSTABS and group counts, means, and sums for MEANS (IBM, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

An independent check is not merely rerunning the same formula. Hand-count IDs 101–106, verify five on-time outcomes, and add their six prep values. Then reconcile SPSS, Excel, and the hand tally. If counts differ, inspect missing categories, filters, duplicate IDs, and whether SPSS has weights active before presenting a rate. A business-intelligence dashboard can later display the same contract, but a polished dashboard does not repair a wrong denominator.

Failure mode: Averaging an already calculated group percentage across unequal-sized groups produces a misleading overall rate. Rebuild the numerator and denominator from order counts.

Try it — ungraded. Without opening either tool, what should the two reminder-group counts sum to, and why?

Explained answer: 6+6=126+6=12. Every displayed order has exactly one of the two reminder labels. A different total signals an unexpected filter, missing value, duplicate, or entry error that must be resolved before comparing rates.

sections.title: 4. Critique the chart, not just its appearance
sections.html: Why these scores: Chart design controls whether an audience sees the denominator, scale, and uncertainty behind a comparison.

sections.title: 4.1 Match chart and scale to the question
sections.short: 4.1. Match chart and scale to th…
sections.html:
Exploratory analysis asks what patterns or errors deserve investigation; explanatory communication selects a checked finding for a specified audience. The first may involve several views. The second should make one bounded point, not pretend the search never happened. NIST describes exploratory analysis as using, often, graphics to reveal structure and anomalies (Heckert & Filliben, 2003).

Imagine a proposed slide titled “Reminders dramatically improve punctuality.” It has two bars of 83.3% and 50.0%, with a vertical axis starting at 45% and no counts. Critique it in four steps. First, its title makes an unsupported causal claim. Second, the truncated bar axis exaggerates the visible difference in bar lengths. Third, six orders per bar are concealed. Fourth, mode differs across the groups. Replace it with a zero-based, directly labeled bar chart titled “On-time share was higher among reminded orders in this 12-order extract.” Label bars Yes: 5/6 (83.3%) and No: 3/6 (50.0%). Add a note: “Selected completed orders; mode mix differs; descriptive only.” Provide the two-row data table beside or below the chart. Penn State describes bar charts and two-way tables for categorical variables (Penn State Department of Statistics, n.d.-b).

A useful chart exposes its comparison base and does not claim more than its data support.

Failure mode: Adding decimal places, bright colors, or a trend line cannot compensate for the wrong comparison or an absent denominator.

Try it — ungraded. A designer proposes one pie chart containing “83.3% reminded” and “50.0% not reminded.” What is wrong?

Explained answer: These are rates with different denominators, not two pieces of one whole. Two labeled bars plus counts make the comparison intelligible.

sections.title: 4.2 Make the display accessible and auditable
sections.html:
A chart must also work for someone who cannot distinguish its colors or see its bars. Use descriptive text labels, readable contrast, and a nearby table of exact values. If the chart is exported as an image, supply a short text alternative identifying the chart and its point, with the detailed values available in adjacent text or a table. W3C’s guidance treats charts as complex images for which a brief identification and fuller description may both be needed (World Wide Web Consortium, n.d.).

For the proposed reminder chart, a short description could be: “Bar chart comparing on-time order shares by reminder status in a 12-order extract.” The adjacent table gives the fuller description: five of six versus three of six, the corresponding percentages, and the selection caveat. A reader can recover the comparison without relying on bar height.

Failure mode: Alt text that says only “bar chart” supplies neither the question nor the values. Conversely, embedding every caveat in a tiny chart footnote makes the caveat easy to miss.

Try it — ungraded. Could a color-only legend of green for “Yes” and red for “No” replace the printed labels?

Explained answer: No. Print “Reminder sent: Yes/No” and the counts directly. Color may reinforce the distinction, but must not be its only carrier.

sections.title: 5. Build a bounded management story
sections.html: Why these scores: A short recommendation is valuable only when its evidence, assumptions, and next check remain visible.

sections.title: 5.1 Who, what, how: the three-minute story
sections.html:
For who, name the operations manager, who can authorize a monitored trial. For what, identify the decision and the evidence that could alter it. For how, choose an opening sentence, one labeled comparison, one limitation, and one next action. A Big Idea is a one-sentence message joining the observed evidence to a bounded action; it is not a slogan that hides qualifications.

Draft the three-minute story in four moves:

  1. Context: Mosaic Pantry wants more on-time handoffs and has proposed an 80% target.
  2. Evidence: Eight of 12 displayed completed orders were on time, or 66.7%. Reminder-Yes orders were 5/6 on time; reminder-No orders were 3/6.
  3. Boundary: The extract is selected and tiny. Pickup and delivery are unevenly represented across reminder groups. The 33.3-point descriptive gap does not measure the reminder’s effect.
  4. Next action: Confirm source timestamps and eligibility. Then consider a limited prospective comparison with a predefined on-time KPI and prep-pressure guardrail.

A defensible Big Idea is: “The extract shows a punctuality gap worth investigating, not a proven reminder benefit; verify the records and design a monitored trial before rollout.” Storyboarding means laying out these moves before making slides. One panel could show the decision, one the labeled comparison, and one the limitations and next action. That structure stops an eye-catching chart from becoming the conclusion by default.

Failure mode: Leading with “Reminders raise on-time delivery by 33.3%” makes a causal and numerical claim this evidence does not support.

Try it — ungraded. Which sentence belongs in a manager-facing opening: “We ran COUNTIFS” or “We cannot yet tell whether reminders improve handoff”?

Explained answer: The second. It addresses the decision boundary. Keep the formula available for inspection in an appendix or analysis file.

sections.title: 5.2 Separate observation, inference, assumption, and recommendation
sections.html:
These four labels prevent a narrative from quietly changing its level of certainty.

  • Observation: In the 12 displayed orders, 5/65/6 reminded and 3/63/6 unreminded orders were on time. This is directly countable.
  • Inference: Whether a similar gap holds for all future eligible orders is unknown. The selected extract cannot establish it.
  • Assumption: The recorded “On time” and “Reminder sent” fields follow the operational definitions and contain no unexamined missing cases. That assumption still needs verification.
  • Recommendation: Do not scale reminders from this table alone. Ask the data owner to audit timestamps, excluded orders, and mode-specific denominators; then plan a limited comparison with guardrail monitoring.

The ethical boundary is practical: use order-level data with minimal identifiers, restrict access, and avoid presenting staff-selected reminders as proof of staff performance or customer behavior. Later sessions provide sampling uncertainty, A/B guardrails, association analysis, and model diagnostics. None should be smuggled into today’s descriptive result.

Failure mode: A recommendation can be appropriately cautious yet still fail if nobody owns its next step. Here the operations manager can request the audit, while the data owner must document definitions and exclusions.

Try it — ungraded. Label this statement: “All eligible orders next month will show the same 33.3-point gap.”

Explained answer: It is an unsupported inference, not an observation. The observed gap describes only the displayed orders; the extract’s selection and group imbalance make that forecast especially fragile.

sections.title: Recap
sections.html:
• Start with a stakeholder’s decision and the action the analysis might enable.
  • Write a KPI contract: eligible population, time window, grain, numerator, denominator, exclusions, and units.
  • Pair an improvement target with a defined guardrail; label invented thresholds as provisional.
  • One order per row does not mean one row per customer or per message.
  • Check measurement rules and provenance before trusting a correct-looking calculation.
  • Compare groups using their own denominators; show counts beside percentages.
  • Describe an observed gap as a gap, not as causal impact or a forecast.
  • Validate software output against a hand count and source-quality checks.
  • Use a chart whose title, scale, labels, table, and accessibility support its claim.
  • End with a bounded recommendation, the unresolved limits, an owner, and a next action.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
• Basket: Dollar value of one order; $32 for order 101.
  • Categorical variable: A label defining a group; “Pickup” is a mode category.
  • Convenience extract: Records selected because they were readily available; the first 12 completed orders here.
  • Denominator: The eligible cases beneath a rate; six reminder-Yes orders in that group’s rate.
  • Grain: What one row represents; one completed order in this table.
  • Guardrail: A measure that watches for possible harm while pursuing a target; the share with prep over 40 minutes.
  • Inference: A conclusion extending beyond directly observed records; a claim about next month would be one.
  • KPI: A defined measure for monitoring a decision; the on-time handoff rate.
  • Key: A field intended to identify a case uniquely; Order ID at order grain.
  • Numerator: Cases meeting the rate’s condition; eight on-time orders overall.
  • Observation: A recorded case or a directly supported description of cases; order 101 is a case.
  • Operational definition: The rule turning a concept into a field; “at or before recorded promise time” defines on time here.
  • Population: All cases the decision is meant to address; next month’s eligible orders.
  • Provenance: The record of data origins and transformations; which system supplied handoff time and how “On time” was derived.
  • Quantitative variable: A measured amount with meaningful numeric differences; prep minutes.
  • Target: A proposed performance threshold; at least 80% on time in this fictional case.
  • Unit of analysis: The entity counted or compared; an order, not a message.
  • Variable: A characteristic that can differ between cases; reminder status differs between orders.
